questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was important to me to do my study abroad outside of Europe and as I have lived in Asia before, but never South Korea, it was an interesting opportunity for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I struggled a lot to find a university with courses that made sense with my major so I was very limited in my choices.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Korea University sent a lot of information and was very helpful with the application and visa process.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Assistance was much more limited upon arrival. Study portals and course information were primarily in Korean and I had to figure a lot of things out on my own. Korea University has a buddy assistance system (KUBA) where all international students are assigned a Korean student to help them and a bigger group that arranges social events. It is great for the social part but they were little to no help when it came to the navigating Korea and the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Korean students are super nice and want to help you but often they can't because things are different for international students and they simply don't know how things work for us.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I stayed at Kongstay (Jongam location) and I HIGHLY recommend it. I applied in April and had a lot of room options, but others I lived with applied in July and still got a room. Communication was quick and easy and everyone in the administration was super nice.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I stayed in a sharehouse 6 minutes from the university (which is closer than some dorms), and 5 minutes from the metro. Living close to campus was only an issue when getting home between 23.00 and 5.00 as the metro stopped running but otherwise, it was great to live close to the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I highly recommend a sharehouse where you live with other international students so you can share the experiences and struggles of living abroad. No one I knew who lived in the dorms was particularly happy about it. You are not guaranteed a single room and roommates can be very hit or miss. There are also no common areas so it can get very lonely.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course list and registration happen very late and it can be a little unnerving not even knowing which courses will be offered a month before you leave.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course list gets published at the beginning/mid-July and registration opens mid-August. Registration is first come, first serve so it is important to be ready right when it opens as some courses fill up in seconds (not exaggerating). Then the first week of classes is a sort of trial week after which an add-drop period starts and you can drop any class you don't want and sign up for any available ones.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Korea University sends a lot of emails explaining and preparing you for the registration process and it's pretty straightforward.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I initially got pre-approval for 8 courses by UCPH but only 3 of those actually ended up getting offered. After a new search, I found additional courses and ended up getting all but one course that I wanted. Only 1 of the courses I ended up taking was from my original pre-approved list.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you have a lot more courses pre-approved than you need to give yourself enough options.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You will experience courses being taught in Korean even though they are listed to be in English. I had to drop one course because the professor's English was not good enough and one course I was indirectly asked to drop because I was the only non-Korean speaker and it "would just be easier for everyone”. Don't take it personally it is just another reason to have a lot of pre-approved backup courses, and that is what the add-drop period is for.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level felt very much like the level in Copenhagen, if anything not higher.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching is very much based on student participation and I had to do multiple in-class presentations for all of my courses. The only exams I had were term papers that I had all or most of the semester to write, but I think that is only typical for graduate courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Human rights in global and regional context, Approaches to international peace, and Family demography and health.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend “Human rights in global and regional context”, or any human rights course taught by Dr. Jeongeum Choi. Her teaching style is super engaging and I got so much out of her course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The Korean National health insurance is mandatory once you get your ARC. You do get told about it before, but it was more than double what I thought (370kr/m).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries and especially fruit were a lot more expensive than I thought, almost Danish prices. 
Convenience store food is super cheap and really good. Plane tickets to many other Asian countries can be super cheap and I ended up going on a lot more weekend trips than I had planned.
In general I eat out and traveled a lot which is why I ended up spending so much. It can definitely be done cheaper

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: KUBA arranges a lot of dinners and social events, and depending on your buddy they might arrange day trips and other outings in smaller groups. There are supposedly clubs and sports you can participate in, but I don't think it would be possible to know about them or sign up if you don't speak Korean.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
In september there are this big sports competition against Yonsei University and a huge street party afterwards. I am not into sports at all, but it was one of the greatest experiences of my entire exchange.
Definitely rent a Hanbok when you go to the palaces. It is very encouraged even for foreigners and it's a super fun experience.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Of course do a trip to the DMZ.
Try to travel at least a little bit within South Korea, but if you want to go somewhere during Chuseok book it early! Also, try to go somewhere not too popular (like Jeju and Busan) as it gets super crowded with tourists. I went to Jeongju for Chuseok and it turned out to be a super interesting city.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture shock was a lot bigger than I thought it would be and there are a lot of unspoken rules in society I didn't know about.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is difficult if you don't speak Korean. I only had courses with other international students so I only interacted with Korean students at KUBA events.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The general level of English is a lot lower than I expected and apps/websites are almost always only in Korean.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Safety. Both being able to feel safe at night and traveling alone but also Koreans don't steal. People will just leave laptops and wallets on tables and no one ever takes it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Reach out early and make connections whether it is other students from UCPH going to the same university or other international students at Korea University. It's going to make it much easier navigating Korea and the university, and to not feel lonely. Time goes by much faster than you think so don't postpone too much, get out there, and make the experiences. Don't stress too much on the academics, it's all pass/fail in the end.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Try to at least learn how to read Korean before going, even if you don't speak it. A lot of Korean words are just English words spelled with Korean letters so you'll be able to read a lot of signs and menus which is super useful.
If you are able to get an international credit card like WISE definitely do that because Visa/Mastercard will not always work.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I lived with and the friendships I made with people from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Everything is app-based or requires signing up with a Korean phone number. As a non-Korean, you will run into a lot of logistical issues because you either don't have your ARC number or a Korean bank account or phone number, or because those are not properly registered with your ARC number.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
